What is the best consumer level 3D Printer for under $500 that is currently available?

  • By consumer level I mean out of the box ready ** Currently available means you can buy it now

Extra credit: What is the best non consumer level printer available for under $500?

  • in other words a lot of assembly required.
Best consumer level 3D Printer for under $500?

I will jump directly to the extra credit. If one doesn't mind hacking a little bit and electronics are not something scary, then RepRap i3 is a good model. There is a lot of documentation, although a lot of assembly is required. And some previous documentation. For under $500 it should be easy to find some complete kit with good hardware.

I have no experience with "consumer level" printers (nor any friend nor acquaintance with one of them), so I will leave that to other voaters :)
I am not at all put off by electronics, I've been looking over the RepRap's so i3 is a good pick? They look the most versatile and easy to upgrade as well.

I own a version 2 and have learnt a lot and I am very happy with it (well, except the cheap parts, because I bought a quite crappy kit... don't be too cheap on the hardware). It is definitely versatile, and you can upgrade and build/modify your own parts. However, I would say that they would require a lot of time and work to bring you from "have the parts" to "look, mom, I'm printing" ;)

If you are ready to take the time and patience and want to "own" your printer, I recommend it.

I don't think you want a consumer model under $500 dollars.. maybe the new Printrbot Play. The Prusa i3 has been around a bit, but I have seen a lot of problems posted in forums about it. But again, you get what you pay for. It would not be bad to have a lower cost printer that requires more know-how and troubleshooting skill, that's how you learn. And if you don't want to learn, don't even bother. There is nothing about 3d printing that is click and print. Once you have things dialed in, sure. But that's just when something gets out of whack, and your solving a new problem. I think that is going to be with any printer under $1500.

Don't get a prebuilt. You will have to tear it apart to fix it anyway, no printer at any price is hands-off. Save money and preload your 3d printing education by building your machine from the get-go. As an aside you'll get a printer for something like $300 this way.

If you get a cheap prebuilt, prepare for disappointment. You won't know how to fix it, and if your luck is poor your machine will be built by a hungover employee on a friday afternoon right before lunch. Even if your prebuilt is perfect you still won't have a clue what to do when your extruder jams or your bed needs leveling. Just do it all yourself the first time rather than paying extra and doing it all yourself later anyway.

Makerfarm makes good kits that are well reviewed. Follow the documentation, you'll have no trouble. Mechanically they are simple and electronically they are easy. Toughest part is calibration, and by then you have a working printer so the excitement is already there to sustain you. A weekend of building will then have taught you everything you need to know to fix your printer when it goes down (and they all do go down, even the million dollar machines). Added bonus, since you built your first printer so easily, you'll have no fear in printing yourself a second one right away (I recommend a delta for #2).
